name: Bokyi
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Bokyi, in addition to other processes of word formation, uses pitch variations (tone) to determine the meaning of certain words. That is, a particular word in Bokyi can have several meanings depending on the pitch used in its realization. The pitch applies independently to each syllable of the word. [...] In Oshita (2004:107), Tawo (1977: 126) agrees that Bokyi is a tone language. [...] [p.173:] Also, it was noticed that while tone changes the meaning and word class of a word (ie in the derivation of Bokyi adverbs), stress, in English, equally changes the meaning and /or word class of English word [...] Tone in Bokyi and stress in English may therefore be serving a similar function
new_statements.citation: Bisong, M. Tabang & Abubakar Alakli Usman. 2017. Tone and learning of English tenses by Boky learner-users of English. Journal of Language, Literature and Cultural Studies (JOLLACS) 2: 164-175.
new_statements.locator: pp. 168-169 (section '2. Tonality as a word formation process in Bokyi') and p. 173
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (20-page scan, no text layer) and its tesseract text. The quoted passage is at scanned lines 557-565 (pg-013 = printed p.169, section '2. Tonality as a word formation process in Bokyi') and lines 753-767 (pg-017 = printed p.173). I also rendered PDF page 14 (printed p.169) to an image and read it directly: 'Bokyi, in addition to other processes of word formation, uses pitch variations (tone) to determine the meaning of certain words. That is, a particular word in Bokyi can have several meanings depending on the pitch used in its realization. The pitch applies independently to each syllable of the word.... In Oshita (2004:107), Tawo (1977:126) agrees that Bokyi is a tone langua…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bokyi is described as a lexical/grammatical tone language (H, M, L and falling tones illustrated; each syllable carries its own pitch; verb TAM forms distinguished by tone alone). The authors treat 'tone in Bokyi' as the counterpart of 'stress in English'; no location of word stress, and no explicit claim that Bokyi lacks stress, is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None; only tone minimal sets (e.g. bè 'come' L / bé 'marry' H / bē 'we' M; kayang HH 'small animal' / HL 'idiot' / ML 'mosquito') and tonal verb paradigms (okí 'gives', okì 'gave', ókì 'given', ōki 'does not give').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical and grammatical tone in citation forms; the papers are contrastive English-L2 pedagogy studies by a native-speaker linguist, not a phonological description. The tone-language classification is attributed to Tawo(-Asu) 1977:126, the primary grammar sketch, which was not accessible. The same wording recurs in Bisong & Onucheyo 2020 (Morphology of English and Bokyi, pp. 6, 9-10, 118), also saved.
new_statements.identity_note: The Bisong papers describe Bokyi as spoken in Boki LGA, Cross River State (author a native speaker; dialect not specified, examples in the standard Bokyi orthography of Bruns/Tawo-Asu, i.e. essentially the Osokom/Okundi-based written norm). Glottolog boky1238 has 14 dialect nodes; Blench (2026, per Wikipedia) treats Abu/Baswo [aboo1241] as a separate Bendi language, so statements here should not be extended to Abu.

sources.locator: pp. 168-169 (section '2. Tonality as a word formation process in Bokyi') and p. 173
sources.note: Contrastive/pedagogical paper by a native-speaker linguist. pp.168-169: Bokyi is a tone language (citing Tawo 1977:126), 'The pitch applies independently to each syllable of the word', tone tables for nouns and verb forms (H/L/M/falling). p.173: contrasts 'tone in Bokyi' with 'stress in English' as functionally parallel; no statement of where (or whether) word stress falls in Bokyi.

sources.citation: Bisong, M. Tabang & A. F. Onucheyo. 2020. Inflectional processes in English and Bokyi: the pedagogical implications. Lokoja Journal of English and Literature (LOJEL) 1(2): 190-201. (GOUni eprints 3672, whole issue)
sources.note: Same tone-vs-suffixation contrast as the 2017 paper; no stress statement for Bokyi.

sources.citation: Bisong, M. Tabang & Antonio Friday Onucheyo. 2020. Morphology of English and Bokyi. Kogi State: Catholic Media Centre. 153 pp. ISBN 978-92-8209-819-9. (GOUni eprints 3940)
sources.note: pp.6, 9-10: 'Bokyi is a tone language, that is, distinctions in the pitch of a single syllable may realize completely different words or different grammatical functions' (low/high/falling examples); pp.115-118 define syllable/stress/intonation for English only and say 'Tone in Bokyi and stress in English may therefore be serving a similar function'; p.7 summarises Bisong (1994) on English vs Bokyi segment inventories. Nothing on Bokyi stress placement.
